ALLEGED COMMENTS OF MEMBER FOR ROSEMONT
speechtext: Last week, we heard the hon. member for Beauce comment on a newspaper article about the Acting Speaker. After a number of discussions, I think it may be appropriate to hear what the hon. member for Rosemont has to say.

subtopic: ALLEGED COMMENTS OF MEMBER FOR ROSEMONT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Beauce quoted a sentence that was reported in a newspaper obviously out of context.
What people should realize is that we had a big meeting of militant members of the Bloc Quebecois in the riding of Beauport-Montmorency-Orleans, attended by nearly 1,500 people. These people know their member very well, especially since they were largely responsible for electing him in 1984 and 1988. They remember his doubts when he was about to join the Bloc Quebecois when he was in his riding in 19% and 1991, and then went back to the Conservatives in Ottawa.
What I said in addition to what was reported in the press is that by accepting his appointment as one of the Deputy Chairmen of the House, the hon. member for Beauport-Montmorency-Orleans had put himself in a position where he had to apply rules that did not recognize the Bloc Quebecois, with the approval of the traditional political parties here in this House. Of course I realize, and that is why I used the word instrument, that the Speaker cannot overrule a decision by members and party leaders who applied the letter rather than the intent of the Standing Orders, because everyone knows
perfectly well there are precedents that would amply justify recognizing the Bloc Quebecois as a political party.
It is quite simple. The hon. member for Beauport- Montmorency-Orleans had a choice. He made his choice and, as a result of that decision, he is now in a position to apply rules set by all or by almost all political parties in this House, by what we call the traditional parties.
I used the word collusion. Perhaps I should have said coalition, since collusion connotes an element of secrecy.
I may add that the committee's meetings were secret and that we were never able to explain our position. We were never able to discuss it. The Standing Orders were applied. In fact they were used as an excuse and there was never an open debate. I think it would be more accurate to refer to a coalition of the traditional parties in the House instead of collusion.
The crux of the matter remains the same, and the people of Beauport-Montmorency-Orleans realize that. The fact is that for the past two years we have had a situation where many members told their constituents they were very close to the Bloc Quebecois, and now when conventions are being held to elect candidates for the next election people should know where they stand. I think the residents of Beauport-Montmorency- Orleans will know exactly where they stand in the next election.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: ALLEGED COMMENTS OF MEMBER FOR ROSEMONT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I may comment briefly on this point of order. Personally, and I am sure I also speak for most if not all parliamentarians in this House, I think that when presiding over the proceedings of this House the hon. member for Beauport-Montmorency- Orleans is absolutely fair and impartial. If people say the hon. member takes political sides in his own riding, well I certainly hope so. After all, he was elected as a member of a political party. But to say that his role in the Chair makes him party to some kind of collusion or coalition is unfair because it reflects on the Speakership as a whole.

March 23, 1993
Speaker's Ruling
Mr. Speaker, you have said many times that the Speaker is the servant of the House, not its leader. You yourself, Mr. Speaker, are a servant of the House and your colleagues as well, including the hon. member for Beauport-Montmorency-Orleans. I think he is strictly impartial in the performance of his duties and, as I see it, this criticism is entirely unfair. He is no one's instrument. He is, as you are, Mr. Speaker, a servant of this House, and that is as it should be.

subtopic: ALLEGED COMMENTS OF MEMBER FOR ROSEMONT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after listening to the hon. member for Rosemont going on at length about how he was misinterpreted or quoted out of context I still believe the journalists at the Beauport-Ex-press in Beauport-Montmorency-Orleans accurately reported what was said that evening.
There was talk of collusion. It was said that the rights of Bloc Quebecois members were violated in this House. I think the hon. member for Beauport-Montmorency- Orleans is doing a magnificent job in this House as one of its Deputy Chairmen. With unruffled calm and an abiding concern for fairness and justice he has always given everyone his due here in the House.
Since the hon. member for Rosemont is apparently unwilling to admit that he went too far-although it would have been so easy for him do so this morning-I wish to move, seconded by the hon. member for Terrebonne:
That the matter of the comments made by Mr. Tremblay, member for Rosemont, with regard to Mr. DeBlois, member for Beauport - Montmorency-Orleans and Assistant Deputy Chairman of Committees of the Whole, as reported in the March 14, 1993 edition of the newspaper Beauport-Express, be referred to the Standing Committee on House Management.
I move this motion, Mr. Speaker, subject to the Chair's ruling.

This is, of course, a rather difficult situation, not only for the Speaker and the hon. member, but also for the House.
I listened carefully to what was said by the hon. member for Rosemont. He may have given some explanation of the circumstances in which he made the
comments that were quoted in the newspaper in question.
However, I have some difficulty with the facts, because clearly if we consider only what was quoted in the newspaper those words are in my opinion unacceptable to this House. If we consider the words that were reported we clearly have a prima facie case that affects the dignity of this House and our colleague, because our colleague is an officer of this House. As the hon. member for Glengany-Prescott-Russell said earlier, like the Speaker he is an officer of this House and an attack against the integrity of a person in that position is an attack against this House.
As I said before, I listened to the comments of the hon. member for Rosemont, and I assume the crux of the problem is the position of the Bloc in this House. I realize that there have been ongoing complaints by some members of the Bloc Quebecois about its status as a party in this House.
However, all members, and the public as well, must realize the decision on the status of members of the Bloc Quebecois was not made by the Speaker or by our colleague.
If the hon. member for Rosemont would accept this distinction and perhaps be willing to withdraw this morning the comments he made with reference to the Speaker-and as the Speaker of this House I am his Speaker as well-we would accept that.
However, in the circumstances, I think that for the sake of relations between Bloc Quebecois members and the other members of this House it would be entirely appropriate to withdraw altogether the comments reported in the newspaper.
If there is a withdrawal, it would be preferable to make it here. I therefore suggest that the hon. member for Rosemont consider the Chair's comments and perhaps, on reflection, he might wish to withdraw entirely the comments that were quoted in the newspaper.

Mr. Speaker, I do not know whether we have a language problem, but I think I made it quite clear that I understood the Speaker did not, and cannot, for that matter, make the rules that denied the Bloc Quebecois recognition as a political party. I made that quite clear.
March 23, 1993

I also said that by accepting the appointment the hon. member was bound to apply rules made by others. If that is interpreted as inferring that decisions made by the hon. member for Beauport-Montmorency-Orleans were not impartial, that certainly is not what I meant. I meant that by accepting this appointment, he put himself in a position where he had to apply rules against the recognition of the Bloc Quebecois, which are not his to change.
As the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell said earlier, he has become a servant of the members of this House. Instead of using the word servant, I used the words un instrument. I do not want that to be interpreted as being partial. When he makes decisions in the House, he cannot do otherwise but apply the non-recognition rule.
My point was that he had the choice to either accept or refuse this position. It is quite clear that he is a servant of the House. I referred to un instrument and I am quite prepared to withdraw the word collusion, if you prefer, and to talk about a coalition, which is common knowledge.
It seems to me my interpretation is quite clear, and people know, as the hon. member for Glengarry-Pres-cott-Russell said earlier, that the Speaker is a servant of the House.

First of all, I want to thank the hon. member for his comments and his explanation, but there still is a problem. Although the hon. member for Rosemont has put forward certain arguments which are not altogether impossible to understand, especially in politics, I still think we are faced with a difficult situation for the House.

Consequently, having found there is a prima facie case I am going to put the motion of the hon. member for Beauce to the House. Then it will be for the committee and the House to decide. The hon. member for Rosemont will of course have a chance to discuss the matter with his colleagues in the House and in the committee.
It may well be that out of that discussion may come something useful in terms of the general amity of
Routine Proceedings
members among themselves. I do think it is a matter for the House to decide.
The House has heard the terms of the motion. Is there agreement?
Agreed.
Motion agreed to.

Mr. Speaker, you said that you had some difficulty. I am trying to understand what that difficulty is because I think I clearly explained that what I said was not a reflection on the decisions of the Speaker. I explained that I would substitute the word coalition, a decision by all the members of this House, for the word collusion. I am trying to understand your reasons for this decision, Mr. Speaker, and I must say, quite honestly, that I am somewhat at a loss.

The hon. member for Rosemont will understand it is not appropriate for the Chair to give an explanation after making its decision. However, I suggested he withdraw his remarks as reported in the newspaper. The hon. member may not agree with the Chair's suggestion, but lacking a specific statement by the hon. member in which he withdraws his words I believe it is appropriate to give the House and the committee an opportunity to consider this matter. The hon. member has every right to state his case, and he will have ample opportunity to do so in committee. After this brief explanation I think the case is closed. Once the committee has tabled its report the House may have a chance to consider the matter again. However, for the time being the case is closed.

The House resumed from Friday, March 19, consideration of Bill C-113, an act to provide for government expenditure restraint, as reported (without amendment) from a legislative committee; and Motions Nos. 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 13 and 14.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague, the member for Timmins-Chapleau, for the amendments he has introduced to the unemployment insurance section of Bill C-113.

March 23, 1993
Government Orders
The legislation is so terrible that nothing can really make it palatable, but if we can in some small way lessen some of the effects of the bill, that at least is a worth-while exercise.
I understand that government members are being inflexible in their approach to the amendments, but I hope they will take a serious look at them and will actually choose to support some of the improvements to the impacts the bill will have.
There are a number of amendments dealing with clause 18 of the bill. This clause increases the grounds for just cause. The first paragraph of the bill suggests that just cause exists where the claimant has no reasonable alternative to leaving employment. Motion No. 7 would replace that phrase so the just cause for leaving employment exists where any of the following circumstances applied to the claimant.
The reasonable alternative is out, that the government provides for itself. In the "but book", the book of draft directives issued by the director of benefit entitlements, every legitimate reason for quitting a job also has a number of buts applied to it. You can quit your job to look after a child, but only if you first ask a trusted relative or if you have asked for a change of hours, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera.
Even the new briefing book listing reasonable alternatives to go with every just cause provided the commission with a means of rejecting claimants, even though they have given just cause reasons for quitting.
Motion No. 8 adds reasons for just cause, bringing the total to 40. The Conservatives like to tell us that jurisprudence actually gives us 40 reasons that provide just cause. They speak of these 40 reasons in tones of reassurance. Why should we worry about people being unfairly penalized when there are all these reasons they can use to get benefits.
We have basically included all 40 to call their bluff. We notice the parliamentary secretary for finance said on Friday that he recognizes this as an attempt to expand the definition of just cause, but he calls the motion unnecessary because the 13 reasons listed already cover the vast majority of additional reasons proposed by the member. That is what he says.
In other words, the 40 reasons with which the government has attempted to reassure Canadians do not really have any weight at all. Most are variations of the original five already in the UI act.
It is true there is some minimal advantage in increasing the list to 40, just as there is some minimal advantage in increasing the list to 14. They may be a little stronger for being there but they should not be looked at in a simplistic manner. It cannot be said that because the reason is on the list one gets the benefits.
We have case after case which demonstrates how people listed these reasons and still lost the benefits. There are inconsistencies now in the application of the just cause penalties at the level of the agent, the appeal board or the umpire. It is the umpire level which establishes the new jurisprudence. In the future people will lose all their benefits because of some factor buried in the existing law which basically says a good reason is not good enough.
The last reason in our amendment does not include "as prescribed" which appeared in the bill. As prescribed pertains to jurisprudence and commission regulations. If these two words go into the new legislation, a truly just cause will not be considered if it is not contained in the jurisprudence and commission regulations. It limits any future additions to jurisprudence.
Motion No. 9 places the onus of proof with the commission and establishes that benefit of doubt beyond any reasonable doubt shall go to the claimant. In spite of the commission's continual assurance that the benefit of doubt will be given to the claimant, there is nothing in the act that says this. There is also nothing to reverse the onus of proof to the commission. Under the present practice the claimants must prove they had just cause rather than the commission proving they did not.
Motion No. 10 clarifies that a common law spouse is a spouse under the act. That should not be necessary as one would think that common law relationships are now fully recognized. However, we can show an umpire's decision which states that if Parliament in its wisdom had wanted to include-and I believe it should be included that it would be just cause to quit one's job to follow a common law spouse-Parliament would have stated so in the statute.
The parliamentary secretary smugly suggested this amendment was not necessary because UIC guidelines now include common law spouses. I remind him in the presence of legislation it is jurisprudence that establishes the rules. Because of this umpire's decision the policy should become stricter. Here is our opportunity to include it if members of the other side of the House will only support this motion.
March 23, 1993

Clause 20 of the bill amends section 30.1 of the UI act so that claimants disqualified on the basis of section 28 will lose all their benefits. Section 28 claimants are those who are fired for misconduct or who quit without just cause. These same claimants lose seven to twelve weeks of benefits and their benefits after that are reduced to 50 per cent.
Our position is that this penalty is severe enough. With that kind of penalty very few people would quit a job just for the fun of it, particularly in an economy where they risk getting no job again.
The minister likes to ask if anyone who quits a job without good reason should get UI. I would like to ask the minister: Does he believe workers who had good reasons for quitting their jobs should still lose all their benefits? Under this law that is exactly what is going to happen. No one really deserves to lose all benefits. The worst part of this legislation is that many of these people will be innocent victims; people who will not be able to prove their case. We all know that under this system you are guilty until you prove yourself innocent.
We are calling Motion No. 13 the Quebec amendment. As suggested by some Conservative members from Quebec, the bill as it stands now is too inhumane. We therefore suggest a three-step process. The first time a person is fired is the first event. The claimant remains under the current legislation of seven to twelve week exclusions. If there is a second event a person gets the maximum 12 week exclusion. Only if there is a third event will the claimant suffer a total loss of benefits. Motion No. 11 is included as cross-referencing for the purpose of the Quebec amendment. These corrections would have to be made to make Motion No. 13 apply.
This is the essence of the amendment the Quebec Tories who protested Bill C-105 wanted to see. We are putting it in for them. Allowing workers three chances obviously is more humane. While we in no way agree that it would make the bill acceptable, as with any of the amendments it is obviously better that total loss of benefits should not be the penalty until someone has quit or been fired on three successive occasions.
Government Orders
Under clause 20(4), once a person is disqualified none of the insurable weeks of employment prior to the event can be used to requalify for a later claim. I am running out of time but I would like to point out that with respect to time which has been earned previously and has not been used up in no way under any circumstances should the person be disqualified from using it. This is simply overkill. It is using a shotgun to kill flies and there are many other analogies one could make.
I hope that the minister and the government members will consider their opposition to these amendments as I believe they make vital corrections. The impact of this bill will be incredibly severe. Surely the government cannot object to some amendments which will soften it.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to take part in this debate at report stage. I have one or two points I want to make. I know a lot has been said on both sides of the House and I know that members on this side have for the past several weeks condemned Bill C-113, particularly as it relates to unemployment insurance.
I have been involved in UI debates for many years and if there is one area of law making that increases the intensity of debate around here, it is amendments from time to time in relation to the Unemployment Insurance Commission.
Every government we have had in the 22 years I have been a member of this House has in its so-called reform approach to UI come in with measures that are ever more Draconian. For example, the Liberals a number of years ago reduced benefits from 66 per cent of income down to 60 per cent of income. Now they are screaming because the Conservative government is about to reduce the benefits from 60 per cent to 57 per cent.
There is no doubt in my mind that the Conservative government is using the Unemployment Insurance Act as a weapon in its arsenal for deficit reduction but it is doing it on the backs of the unemployed. That is simply not fair.
I am a member not of the labour committee but of the justice committee of this House. I cannot help but draw certain parallels between the Unemployment Insurance Commission and how it operates and the criminal justice system in this country and how it operates.

Government Orders
In the criminal justice system the onus of proof of guilt is on the system. In other words the Crown has to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused is guilty. The accused does not have to prove his or her innocence.
In the unemployment insurance system it is just the opposite. The onus of proof is on the claimant. When the claimant is adjudicated and there is any doubt whether or not his or her claim should be acceptable, and the Unemployment Insurance Commission says it is not acceptable, then the onus of proof is on the claimant. The onus of proof is on the person applying for the unemployment insurance.
Incidentally this is not a welfare system. This is an insurance system. It is a compulsory insurance system into which the claimant has been forced by statute to pay. It is an insurance against loss of income due to being unemployed. But at the same time the government insists that the claimant must prove that the claim is correct. It is not the other way around. It is philosophically unfair. It is basically unfair at the outset.
Second, in the criminal justice system, a person is innocent until proven guilty, as I mentioned a few moments ago. It is often an assumption in the unemployment insurance system if there is a very deeply disputed aspect that the claimant is guilty until proven innocent. This is very often involved in disputes arising from being dismissed for just cause or quitting for just cause.
Third, the criminal justice system is guided by laws that must be changed by statute. This is a very rigorous process. The unemployment insurance system is guided by directives that can be changed by the commission at any time, that can be interpreted loosely or severely, depending very often on the individuals who are involved in the actual hearing itself. Consequently in the UI system, many of the decisions are based upon individual officers in the commission itself, not according to law, not even according to regulations sometimes, but according to a whim, or according to a very narrow interpretation.
Fourth, in the criminal justice system all witnesses are treated equally before the law. That is a basic precept. The odd time this does not occur, it usually gets front page coverage, particularly in the criminal justice system
if it involves a person who has been charged with a serious offence. In the unemployment insurance system, employers have more power than the claimants through the separation slip and through the approach recommended by the UI directives. I do not think there is any question about this. In a dispute between an employer and an employee the decision goes in favour of the employer most of the time.
Fifth, under the criminal justice system decisions are made first by police that investigate a crime and gather information and evidence. They present the evidence to a Crown prosecutor. It is a decision of the Crown prosecutor whether to proceed with the charges or not. Then the trial itself involves prosecution, defence, the judge-that is the bench-as well as a jury very often. However, in the unemployment insurance regime the UI agent is the police officer, the lawyer and the judge, usually with the responsibility for making a decision alone. We are speaking here of the decision of first instance.
In the criminal justice system, except in extreme crimes, jail sentences or fines are not imposed until after the appeal system has been exhausted. The fine or the jail sentence may be arrived at in court and prescribed, but the fine is not paid or the jail term is not served until all the appeal processes have been exhausted.
In the unemployment insurance system the claimant suffers total loss of income immediately. What does the claimant live on while pursuing the appeal? This is particularly true in cases of alleged sexual harassment. It is easy for the government to say all the person has to do is launch an appeal if there is any doubt whether or not sexual harassment was a factor in a person leaving her job. That is fair enough. The point here is it may take months, in fact I have heard of some cases taking over a couple of years to resolve. In the meantime, that person is not receiving any benefits from the Unemployment Insurance Commission into which that person has had to contribute by statute. To me that is not fair.
Again, under the criminal justice system, sentences to fit the crime may increase or decrease minimally within a prescribed range. Under Bill C-113 the penalty goes from a maximum of 12 weeks' loss of income to full loss of income. I argue that is not fair.

In the criminal justice system though inconsistency exists in the system it is controlled by the appeal process. If mistakes have been made at the lower level, at the court of first instance, the appeal system is there to correct the inconsistencies or the mistakes that were made.
In the unemployment insurance system decisions from one employment centre to another can differ greatly. Appeals are also localized and potentially inconsistent. There is very little one can do about it, if anything.
Again under the criminal justice system if an appeal process is too lengthy the court may drop charges against the defendant. That happened in the province of Ontario a couple of years ago. Many charges, some of them fairly serious, were stayed simply because the courts were technically unable to receive and do their job. They were backlogged to the point where the Supreme Court of Canada said that it was not fair to keep the charges outstanding and therefore they were stayed.
Under the unemployment insurance system there are no regulations which proclaim a minimum appeal time in favour of the claimant.
Again I go back to the sexual harassment aspect of an unemployment insurance appeal. Why should a woman who says that she was sexually harassed and therefore was forced to quit her job have to wait for months, even up to two years to get justice in the unemployment insurance system and at the same time receive no benefits if in the criminal justice system there are prescribed limits of time after which the charges must be stayed? Justice delayed is justice denied. Surely the same principle should apply in the unemployment insurance system.
Finally, in the criminal justice system the defendant cannot be excluded from his or her trial except in cases of extreme misbehaviour in the actual court proceedings. Under the unemployment insurance system, Bill C-113 allows the chair of an appeal board to exclude the claimant while hearing evidence from the employer.
For some or all of those reasons, I am voting against Bill C-113.
Government Orders

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure in some respects to at least stand and discuss this particular bill and point out some of the errors the government has made with respect to UI legislation.
I think all of us when we first heard that a bill was coming down-I think it was Bill C-105-looked at the general intent and said it was a good idea to look at unemployment insurance. We could see if there were ways to improve the system to make it work better and to make sure that it was not being defrauded or abused.
When we finally had a chance to analyse the bill it became very clear the bill was lacking. In fact the government knew it was lacking as well because it withdrew the bill and made many amendments and changes to try to make it look better.
The optics of correcting abuse in the UI system is always great. Anybody who works hates to think that their tax dollars are going to somebody who is freeload-ing or abusing the system or who is actually taking from the system unjustifiably.
It is great optics from the government's point of view to proceed on that basis and introduce this legislation, but it knew it was wrong. The government made changes. It has now brought back another bills which is what we are debating today, and the same problems are still there.
I think the government now is a little worried that the optics have gone a little sour. In fact, when we really analyse what has happened here the government is saying that it has a major political problem. There are 1.6 million Canadians out of work and of those about
400,000	are youth. The government is saying: "We cannot deal with it. We do not have any answers. We are stuck. We are finished. We do not understand. We cannot do anything. What do we do? Rather than trying to deal with the situation let us take a look at the optics again and see if we can come up with something that is just a little neater and divert people's attention".
I am sure everyone is familiar with the old shell game where you hide the pea and try to divert people's attention away from what is going on so that they cannot figure out where the pea is.

March 23, 1993
Government Orders
The simple fact of the matter is that is what is going on here with Bill C-113. The government is trying to divert Canadians' attention away from the problem of unemployment and put it on the backs of unemployment insurance and the small number of people who may be abusing the system.

The unemployment insurance program is the federal government's single largest expenditure, forecast to be $22.5 billion for 1993. Before 1990 the federal government's contribution to the UI fund was approximately 20 per cent, and since that time it is now totally financed by employees and employers. As a result of rising UI costs the UI fund has a deficit of $4.7 billion. I have already read into the record how the government could have reduced that.
The government expects that cutting the benefit rate from 60 to 57 per cent will save a total of $2.45 billion over two years. Maybe so, but at what cost?
How does the government justify these cuts? It says that these cuts are necessary to stop all those shiftless, irresponsible people who quit their jobs and then expect to be supported by hard-working responsible Canadians. But how many people are actually abusing the system? I would like to suggest there are not too many. There are two kinds of abuse. There are those who defraud the system with false claims and other scams and there are people who receive benefits after quitting their jobs for no apparent reason or after being fired.
The government calls the first group the cheaters. According to its own statistics the amount of money that is lost annually to these cheaters is something like $200 million, or less than 1 per cent of the total program. It is not a great amount of money.
The government estimates that 6 per cent of UI recipients are people who either left their jobs without just cause or were fired for misconduct. It has been shown by a great number of people that the measures proposed in Bill C-113 will not reduce or even contain the deficit of the UI fund. The government is simply cutting for the sake of cutting without any all-encompassing vision of what the UI program should be doing or any idea of how the program could be made to work better.
The government does not know what to do about Canada's unemployment crisis, and that is the major problem. If the proposed changes in Bill C-113 become law then those people no longer eligible for UI will have to turn to the already over-taxed welfare system.
Let me relate this to the Ottawa-Carleton region, of which Nepean is part. At the start of this month there were 30,300 unemployed persons in the RMOC.
Changes to unemployment insurance are being felt in all sectors of this community.
The message from Canadians, as well as the people in this region, is that the changes to UI must not be taken as a simple budgetary measure but must be viewed in the context of a broader change affecting elements of our social safety net. They also go on to say that between 1990 and 1992 the number of unemployed persons in the RMOC increased by 10,800, or 64 per cent.
During the same period the number of social assistance case-loads had increased by an average of 540 per month, including a 345 per month increase in case-loads of employable persons. Changes in UI will mean that employable persons will remain on welfare longer. Approximately 6 per cent of all the UI claimants in the region quit their jobs. This means that as many as 1,350 individuals of the RMOC who are eligible for UI benefits in the present system will not be eligible for UI in April 1993.
Provincial and regional governments will experience increased financial burden as a result of changes to the UI law. The decrease in the number of people eligible for UI could mean a loss of $16,452 million per year in gross UI benefits to this region of Ottawa-Carleton. That is an incredible amount of money.
In addition, the reduction of the benefit rate from 60 to 57 per cent will mean a further annual loss of $24,684 million to the region in UI benefits. At the same time, contributions to the provinces and municipalities for social programs have not kept pace with the increased financial burdens they have experienced.
I mentioned this because it is having a very grave impact upon all of the municipalities across the country. It is clearly a case of shifting the burden from one level of government to the other and yet it is the same taxpayer who is footing the bill for them all.
The major criticisms that people have levelled at these changes are that people will be much less likely to quit their jobs, regardless of the working conditions, because they will no longer be eligible for UI; and employers will be able to use the threat of dismissal to force employees to accept a situation that might otherwise have met with resistance. Mr. Speaker, I join the member who just spoke in hoping that everyone will vote against this bill, but I am not very confident that will happen.
Some four years ago the government embarked upon a program to slow down what it called the overheated economy in southern Ontario. The method it used was to very gradually increase interest rates, so gradually that it had little effect on the economy in southern Ontario or anywhere else because what kept the economy going was the increasing amount of credit that was available. As long as the lenders were prepared to give that credit businesses kept borrowing. As long as the money was being spent and businesses were expanding workers were getting money, spending that money and buying the goods that were being produced, and the economy kept growing at a great rate.
Government Orders
It was only when the lenders started to worry about collecting the money they had loaned out that the economy started to slow down. However it did not slow down as gradually as the interest rates had gone up. It slowed down precipitously, so that we entered the period that the Conference Board of Canada described as the first ever recession in Canada created by government policy. The government did it not by increasing interest rates but by increasing them to the point where the lenders started to worry about collecting their money back. The money was no longer in circulation and people no longer had the funds to buy the goods that were being produced in Canada, and we now have what some call a recession and what some know is a depression.
The government has learned nothing from that experience because we are now at the point where it wants to get the economy moving again. What does it do? It lowers interest rates. But again, it is doing it so gradually that it has little effect on the economy. It will not have any effect until it gets to the point where the lenders are confident about getting back the money that they lend out. They are not going to do that until Canadians start purchasing again.
It is hoped that this legislation before us now in part will save the UI fund some $500 million to $600 million this year. It may save the UI fund but, as others have pointed out by downloading these costs onto the provincial governments and reducing the amount of money that will be available, when people change from UI to welfare they will be getting less.
It is not just that people are getting less but that people are losing whatever confidence they might have had in any kind of a recovery.
When we see headlines from time to time saying that there are signs that the economy is turning around, fewer and fewer people believe that it really is turning around because they do not see it and they do not feel it. They know that the number of unemployed is increasing. They know that the number of jobs is decreasing, that is, the well-paying jobs, the ones that really count.

From time to time we see stories of plants shutting down or plants, businesses and industry moving away from Canada to the sunnier climes of Mexico.
The government may well save the UI fund $500 million-I do not know, I understand that figure is questionable-but it is taking it from the people who can least afford to fight the recession and the depression. Those are the people who are already not earning very much, if they are earning at all. Those are the people who would be spending every cent that they received in their own communities throughout Canada, and by spending it would give some encouragement to people who are in business and give some encouragement to the people who are working, so that they can spend their savings in some security of the job which they hope will continue.
Now they have little of that because more and more people are worried that if others are losing their jobs, when will it be their turn?
Until the recovery does become a reality people are not going to have the confidence they need to spend their savings to get the economy moving, or to even spend their earnings.
We are taking it from the poorest. The people who have lost their jobs are now going to have something like a 10 per cent reduction in the amount of UI they can claim. If they do claim UI they will not know whether they are going to get it because there will be tests. They will have to undergo examinations to see whether or not they qualify for UI.
I do not mind that kind of checking up, but the purpose of it, which is to take more money out of the economy at a time when the economy needs it most, is the crazy part of this measure. It is the same as when the government seemed to have little idea as to how to slow down what it considered to be an overheated economy. It only happened by accident. It did not happen because of the gradual increase in interest rates; it only happened at the point where the lenders were afraid to lend any more.
Once again, it is reducing interest rates gradually, but it is having no effect. When there is some conscious effort on the part of government itself or if industry and business by some miracle get back some of the confidence they have lost in the Canadian economy, only then will it turn around.
In the meantime the government should be doing its share. The government should be taking the lead in providing job opportunities, just like the New Democratic Party which has presented a policy to create employment and put that money into circulation. People who are working are paying income tax. They are paying into the UI fund, not drawing out of it. They are not cutting back, they are expanding.
Putting people to work is the way to reduce the deficit, and eventually to reduce the debt. That is the only answer to the economic problems we have today and the only way we can do that is to bring back confidence. The only way we can bring back confidence is for the government to take the lead quickly, not gradually, not slowly, not in the way it slowed down the economy, not in the way it is trying to improve it right now. It must take dramatic steps to show that the government itself has faith in the future of Canada.
We have talked about an infrastructure program. We have talked about it in the last two federal campaigns in particular. The Liberals picked up part of the idea in the last federal campaign and we will be talking about it again in the coming campaign.
There is a tremendous amount of work that needs doing in this country. We should be hiring contractors in this country, not contractors in other countries who might produce $5.75 billion worth of helicopters. Contractors in this country could be building roads, sidewalks, sewer systems, water systems, things that are needed, upgrading what needs to be done in Canada, projects that would create employment from one end of the country to the other. Yet the government's attitude is that we have to draw in, we have to rein in, we have to control the spending.
By controlling the spending it is doing exactly the wrong thing if it wants to get the economy going again. It should know that. It has had a couple years of experience of gradually going downhill, with the occasional headline saying that things are turning around, things are getting better, knowing full well they are not. The real statistics show the number of people employed in good jobs that enable them to pay substantial income taxes and to pay into UI funds so that the money will be there to draw out for the emergencies some people experience. There is a way to improve our economy. As I stated, more than anything else it depends upon confidence.

To get business moving depends upon the confidence of the lenders to put money into the communities. It depends upon useful work being done, not paying people to stay home on welfare, not paying people to stay on UI, but providing them with useful jobs, especially for the lower income people. They are going to spend that money in their own communities in our country, consuming goods that are produced here in Canada, keeping the money circulating in Canada, and above all else creating some confidence that the government at last has some idea as to what it should do to get the Canadian economy moving again.
It can be done, but the government has to be willing and determined. The government has to show that at last it knows what needs to be done, that it knows the cure for the illness of the Canadian economy and is determined to make that cure available to the Canadian people and the Canadian economy.

far more vulnerable than they are now because of these changes.

All this law does is punish the unemployed for this government's inefficiency. We need programs to help the people of Saint-Laurent-Cartierville find permanent employment. We in the Liberal Party are proposing a new direction for the Canadian economy that would put Canadians back to work. If the Conservatives can no longer lead, we are ready to meet the challenge.

Just before closing, I would like to quote our critic when he said: "If the government is serious about controlling its spending why does it not scale down or cancel its plan to spend $4.4 billion on a submarinehunting helicopter? If the government is serious about wanting to put its financial house in order, why does it not go after the $16.1 billion that Canadian companies have hidden in tax havens such as Barbados, Cyprus, Liberia and elsewhere?
The fact is that this government has no clear plan for controlling its spending and now the most vulnerable Canadians are being forced to pay for its economic mismanagement. The government has a moral responsibility to show Canadians how it intends to prepare our nation for the future. With this bill it has abdicated that responsibility".
That is a quote from our critic, the hon. member for York North.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on behalf of my party, the NDP, to speak on this bill.
You will notice that the government is not defending the bill today. It is not even listening to a number of very serious amendments that have been put forward by the member for Timmins-Chapleau who is trying to take a bad bill and make it a little less so. He has a number of amendments which I am going to speak to in a moment.
Where is the government? It is not doing anything on this bill. The member from Nanaimo spoke for the NDP a few minutes ago and went into the general causes of the economic recession. He accused the government of taking out its inability to put the economy back on a sure footing in this country by tackling the poor and the working stiffs. That is what this government is doing and what this bill does.
We heard the NDP member for Brant speak earlier. He is the critic for the Solicitor General and he said criminals have more rights now than the poor claimants under unemployment insurance. He pointed out that in criminal law a person is innocent until proven guilty but in this system which, as he pointed out, is an insurance system the onus of proof is reversed. We are now making it harder and harder for the ordinary working stiffs to get unemployment insurance after they lose their jobs.

March 23, 1993

My constituents are in Port Moody-Coquitlam, a suburb of Vancouver, British Columbia. Many of them are working, but many are concerned about losing their jobs. When they lose their jobs and go on unemployment insurance-which they have paid into and are paying a heck of a lot more money into thanks to this government-they want to be able to collect. They want the system to operate in a hassle-free way. I will return to that in a moment.
It was interesting to hear members of the Liberal Party speak to advance some policy. Today is Tbesday so the policy is a little different than it was on Monday, but on Wednesday it will be different again. Canadians are beginning to see that the party is self-destructing inside. They are also beginning to see the Liberal Party members on every side of every issue. It is amazing. Now they are wetting their pants, if I might say so, because the Conservatives are changing their leader. It is pretty pathetic. When I heard the member for Parkdale-High Park speak I thought how pathetic that party really is.
The member for Timmins-Chapleau has suggested a number of amendments. I draw this to the attention of the House and the government.
Motion No. 7 would replace the phrase "reasonable alternative". The claimant had no reasonable alternative to leaving employment. Motion No. 7 would replace that phrase so just cause for leaving employment exists "for any of the following circumstances applied to the claimant". It goes on to deal with that. I challenge the government to look at this amendment seriously and agree to it if it wants to help the ordinary working person in this country.
Motion No. 8 adds reasons for just cause bringing the total to 40, which the government claimed and talked about. There it is. Yet the government does not seem to be prepared to accept it.
Motion No. 9 places the onus of proof on the commission and establishes that the benefit of doubt that is beyond reasonable doubt goes to the claimant. As the member for Brant said, why should it be easier for a criminal than a claimant? When in this country are we going to stick up for the ordinary working person?
Motion No. 10 clarifies that a common-law spouse is a spouse under the act. Just on that particular motion, it is not clear now what a common-law spouse is. Here is the decision by an umpire dated in Ottawa on October 2,
Government Orders
1992 concerning the case of Ms. Frances Barzan. The umpire says:
If Parliament, in its wisdom, wanted to include, and I believe it should be so included, that it would be "just cause" to quit one's job to follow a "common-law spouse" Parliament would have so stated in the statute. Parliament has failed to do so and it is not for the umpire to do so. It is not for an umpire to expand the meaning of the word -
But he says he thinks Parliament should. Well here is the amendment. Here is the chance. What is the government waiting for? It should jump at the chance. That is what one of our amendments here deals with.
Here is another decision. I will not cite the name of the applicant, I will just use the initials, E.H. It is a decision by the Federal Court of Canada, Mr. Justice Muldoon, arising from an appeal from Hamilton, Ontario on January 11, 1991. He says this is, and I use the judge's words, "a pathetic case". The poor guy has had to live on the job site to work seven days a week. His back is gone. He leaves his job and Mr. Justice Muldoon makes sure he is allowed an appeal. He deals with it and says he only has to wait one week. Now with this new legislation that is gone. The poor guy would not get UI.
This bill is a tragedy. This is in fact taking it out on ordinary people.
I want to take a little different tack. I have gone through the number of motions. This is an insurance scheme. People pay into this and they pay a lot into it. We MPs, and I think I speak for a lot of members in the House, are getting more and more phone calls in our ridings. My riding office in Coquitlam today, as I speak, is getting phone calls about people whose cheques are delayed, who are not getting it or have to appeal and so on.
We treat these issues as priorities. Just think of the people trying to support their families. They go on UI and have no money even though they have paid into it. They do not want to go to welfare. They want to get their UI quickly and get back to work. They have paid for their UI, so we treat this as a priority in my riding and in other ridings.
We are lucky because we have a phone line to UI. We phone and try to get the case brought forward and so on. It occurs to me that politicians and this government are so unpopular, in spite of the little blip in the polls right at the moment, because they are not working for people any more.
You do not have to be a rocket scientist to analyse this. It is a simple thing like not getting your UI cheque on time, not being treated right and being faced with an impossible bureaucratic appeal process. In immigration it means not having a chance to bring your relative over

March 23, 1993
Government Orders
for the wedding because the visa is delayed. It means the post office. You cannot believe the number of complaints I get every day about the way the post office is working.
This is not complicated. It is just simply making government work for people. That is what people want. They pay for it and they want government to deliver on it.
I want to say this to the employees of the unemployment insurance and immigration offices. I appreciate that they are under stress and they are under strain. They have been cut back by the government and we have 11 per cent unemployment. They have more and more people coming to them. It is tough to provide good service. I know they try very hard.
I also know that they have one of the worst ministers that I have ever seen in the job in my 13 years in Parliament. He is a little blow-hard who thinks he is a mini-Mulroney. He is an ineffective minister. I would not want to work in his department. It must be very tough. I think he is pretty ineffective. I am speaking of the Minister of Employment and Immigration.
The other reason it is hard for the Public Service employees in these offices is that there is a continued attack by the Conservative government on the notion of government. It wants to leave it all to the private sector. It says that government itself is bad. It pulls the wool over the eyes of people.
I say to Canadians and to this House, let us wake up and realize that what people want is government to work for people. Here we are making a UI system that is going to be even harder on people. We have a recession. We have problems with the government deficit. Instead of dealing with the deficit, instead of dealing properly with government spending and waste, instead of dealing with putting people back to work and dealing with the problems of interest rates, a proper trade policy and a proper taxation system so that the middle class does not get burned and burned, what does this government do? It ends up attacking the worker and the poor stiff who loses his or her job and makes it hard to collect UI.
I suggest the government look at these amendments seriously.

Mr. Speaker, I have just a few words on this bill and the amendment before the House.
It is a very serious matter to try to figure out what would be a good reason for quitting employment, what would be just cause. You might think, Mr. Speaker, that something would be a good reason or a just cause and I may not think that would be a good reason or a just cause. It is a very serious and complex matter.
We have had a system in effect in Canada that has scales of penalty. I would argue in my 10 minutes that that is necessary under our system. What we have is a board to hear your appeal. We have a judge to hear your appeal if you are not content with the board. You have the law and you have members of Parliament here in this House.
I will just take the board for a moment. I was looking at some of the most recent cases under just cause. I looked at a case where a fellow had quit his job in Brandon, Manitoba and had gone to British Columbia because he was not getting very much work during the week and was being paid the minimum wage. The Unemployment Insurance Commission said: "No, you cannot collect your unemployment insurance". He appealed it to the board.
Look at what happened at the board level. At the board level he produced further evidence. What was the further evidence? He advised the commission that he faced imprisonment for 90 days because he did not pay his traffic tickets. He had so many driving offences in Manitoba that he decided to move to British Columbia.
What did the board say to that? It is incredible. The board of referees took the new evidence into consideration and found that for a young man to face a jail sentence was a very frightening prospect and felt he had no alternative but to quit his job, leave his family and friends to avoid prosecution, so therefore he qualified for unemployment insurance. That is the board that the government talks about as such an expert. What it was doing was trying to figure out whether this fellow had a good reason for leaving Manitoba.
March 23, 1993

Can you rely on the judge? Look at the recent case of a judge who in 1992 sat in judgment of a lady who had quit because of religious convictions. She was working. Her shift had been changed so she had to work all during the day. It was against her religious convictions to work on that day.
A judge can only deal with the law, can he not? The judge made a ruling. He said: "Look, the fact that I might have been persuaded to have come to a different conclusion, had I been trying the matter in the first instance"-but he was not, the board was. What was his conclusion? "While I have the utmost sympathy for the claimant and respect for the undoubted sincerity of her religious convictions, I am nonetheless obliged to dismiss her appeal". The judge knew that it was wrong. You cannot depend on the judge, can you, in certain cases.
Can you depend on the law? When you walk in, you have got just cause. The law says: "You can appeal this to the board of referees if it based its decision on a misinterpretation of the facts". That is not what is in the law. That is what you were given when you got to the Unemployment Insurance Commission. What is in the law?
The law says: "If the board made an erroneous finding of fact in a perverse or capricious manner", a perverse or capricious manner. That is the law. It is not this that is given to an unemployment insurance claimant. A perverse or capricious manner, go and argue that. Tell that to somebody who cannot get their unemployment insurance. They are trying to figure out: "Do I have just cause? Did the board make a decision in a perverse-". What does perverse mean? Perverse, wicked. A capricious manner, was it a whim?
Can you depend on the law? No, you cannot depend on the law. Can you depend on members of Parliament? Looking at this most recent case here under just cause, it deals with misconduct. This guy was fired for reporting his boss, his supervisor, who he claims was stealing things from the company. The appeal was dismissed. He was fired. The board said: "It appears this type of personal work in the company premises has been condoned in the past" and held that the action of the claimant amounted to misconduct because there is no definition of misconduct in the act. You cannot appeal all those cases on misconduct.
Government Orders
Let us get to the heart of the matter now. Can we really depend on members of Parliament on voluntary leaving with just cause? Here is a ruling of a fellow who had serious nosebleeds, health reasons. Silica dust in a plant was causing him nosebleeds. The judge ruled this and the board and the commission: "The jurisprudence is clear that an employee does not have just cause for leaving unless he has other employment to go to or conditions of work are intolerable with no possibility of them being remedied".
Certainly not turning up for work without even advising the employer is unacceptable. Because he left, because he was having nosebleeds and did not follow through on the remedial action, he has no case to anybody, to the board, to the judge, to anybody.
Finally, where are we in this Chamber? Look at perhaps the most recent case of just cause in which a chap was dismissed for accumulating demerit points. It was deemed that he was dismissed properly. The case went to the courts. The court ruled that he was innocent. Meanwhile, he had lost his unemployment insurance. Now, he is out in the cold.
The law says that the employer had just cause because of this, this and this which was not proven. When a court of law says: "No, that is wrong; there was no just cause", there is nothing in the act to then go back and say: "Give that poor man his unemployment insurance".
In conclusion, let me say that we are dealing with human beings who are applying for unemployment insurance, human beings at the board level, human beings in the person of judges of the Federal Court. What can we expect a judge to do? A judge can only follow the law as it is written and interpret it under jurisprudence that has been determined over a period of time. Finally, we are dealing with human beings who make the law. That is where we fall down in this bill. We have to realize we are dealing with human beings at all levels who can make mistakes.
The law must be flexible enough so that people do not get an unfair deal or an unfair hearing. Certainly let us recognize that the boards are not perfect by any means. Neither are the judges and neither are members of Parliament.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague from Newfoundland who put all of these excellent cases before the House. I hope the government has listened to his arguments and will use them as a basis for returning this bill to its own tables or

March 23, 1993
Government Orders
scrapping it altogether. If it is determined to proceed with the bill, it should look at those points and try to amend the bill in a way so that its impact on people will be negligible.
For those who are interested, we are debating the UI bill which deals with the question of reduction of unemployment insurance payments from 60 per cent to 57 per cent effective April 1, 1993.
There is a second segment to the government proposal that deals with people who might quit their job without just cause. Those people will no longer qualify for UI benefits.
As my colleague from Newfoundland has indicated, it is extremely difficult at times to justify what is just cause. We are really going against the basic principles of our justice system that the accused is innocent until proven guilty. The government is reversing this principle when it comes to the unemployed. In other words you have to prove you are not guilty. You go before the board with the assumption that you are guilty and have to prove your innocence.
Perhaps we should look at the question of the board that will be looking at what is just cause and what is not just cause. In 1991 more than 191,000 cases came before the board. The board was able to deal with about 19,000 cases and was able to reverse those cases.
If the government is to proceed with Bill C-113, all we are going to see is a tremendous increase in the number of people who will be appealing their cases before the board trying to justify leaving their place of employment.
The government has been saying over and over again that it is taxpayers' money involved when it comes to the payment of premiums. That is not quite so. The government used to make contributions to the UI account until the year 1990. After that it became the responsibility of both the employee and the employer.
What will be the impact of this bill if it passes? The unemployed will not disappear from the face of the earth. However those hoping to collect unemployment insurance will have to go to another source for income. That is the social welfare system. By passing the UI bill the government is unloading or passing on the responsibility to another level of government, the municipal government.
The people we are talking about are supposedly the quitters. I am going to take one example from here in our city. We have an unemployment rate of approximately 30,000 people. Of those 30,000 people, approximately 6 per cent or 1,800 people have quit their jobs.
If this bill is passed does it mean that these people will not be eligible to collect UI benefits? The cost would be in excess of about $30 million annually. That money would be taken away from our region. The result of this would be that more people will have to rely on the social assistance benefit. As well, when you add to that the reduction of the benefit from 60 per cent to 57 per cent then you will have an addition to the $30 million of quite a few millions. All of that money has been taken away from the local tax base.
It has been the position of the Liberal Party and members of the opposition that the government has to address the heart of the problem which is the question of unemployment. Rather than attacking the unemployed, why do we not focus on employment and on measures to stimulate the economy so we will have more jobs?
The whole idea behind proper employment initiative programs is to promote labour flexibility and mobility. After all, it is unemployment insurance. It is an interim measure that has been put in place in order to help employees move from one job to another. It is only fair that such a measure is mobile and flexible. It has been put in place in order to meet the objectives.
I see we are getting close to one o'clock. I want to leave the House with one thought. Every time we deal with a situation in this House it always seems to be a question of reacting rather than a question of preventing something from happening.
Most of the bills that I have seen over the past four years have been reactive bills. One would suggest that they should have been preventive bills that would stimulate the economy and help reduce the unemployment rate or create jobs. This bill obviously is no different.
For the sake of 1 per cent of the work force that is quitting their jobs or abusing the system the government has put everybody in the same basket. We will not be supporting this bill. It is my hope that the government will review its decision in light of all the comments and recommendations that were made by our caucus and by the community as a whole.
March 23, 1993

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order.
Given the hour, I wonder if we could have consent from the House to call it one o'clock. We do have other members who want to speak.
