Mr. Speaker, during the three years she served in the Department of Justice the member for Vancouver Centre did nothing to fight groups which promote hatred or hate propaganda.

It takes political will to fight racism. We cannot afford the luxury of doing nothing, like the former Minister of Justice who now hopes to be Prime Minister.
The government's own estimates show that the March 21 anti-racism initiative is ineffective. At the same time, the government has cancelled the Race Relations Foundation, slashed anti-racism funding, and has completely ignored the issue of hate or bias crime.
It is time to take these threats seriously. The former justice minister ignored the problem. I hope this one will not.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to applaud the efforts of the Barrie Welcome Centre. As a community service of the Barrie YMCA the Barrie Welcome Centre assists the settlement of immigrants into the Barrie area. In four years the centre has smoothed the cultural transition of over 1,300 immigrants who have come into Simcoe Centre.
The centre provides services such as translation, help with government and legal documents, information on local social services, health care, housing, employment and recreation areas.
The priority of most newcomers is to obtain a working knowledge of English. Currently it provides English grammar lessons to over 60 enthusiastic new Canadians.
Small things like these services provided by the Barrie Welcome Centre help everyone understand our cultural differences. These first steps of understanding will go a long way toward eliminating racism and helping to create a united country.

Mr. Speaker, the minister of minority rights in Pakistan, His Excellency Peter John Sahotra, is now visiting Canada for a few days.
Canadians urge him to ensure maximum protection in Pakistan for Christian and other religious minorities. We hope good relations between our countries will not be marred by an increase in human rights violations in either country.
The Christians, who are less than 1 per cent of the population in Pakistan, were there before the state of Pakistan was founded and have their roots there. Nevertheless, recent violent mobs have attacked Christian clerics and churches, prompting cancellation of some Christmas services.

March 23, 1993
News reports indicate that Christians in some cases have been killed or sentenced to death on false charges of blasphemy against Islam.
We congratulate the Government of Pakistan for abandoning plans to show religious affiliation on citizens' identity cards, which would have opened the way for more discrimination against Christians in lodging and employment.
We call on the Government of Pakistan to fulfil its commitment to provide compensation to the churches that were damaged in riots last year and to provide adequate security in the future, rather than curtailing the rights and freedoms of Christians and other religious minorities.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance; Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government has a strategy which will foster economic recoveiy, and pave the way for the future and will control the deficit. It depends on private sector support, because the private sector will guarantee our future growth.
We know that just stimulating public spending in the hope of stimulating growth does not work. We have many examples of countries that tried to escape the realities of the world economy. Many times we saw them try to throw money into ill-conceived public investments and poorly designed job creation programs. Many times they have had to retreat, cut spending and get their finances back in order. This has happened in France, in Great Britain and more recently in Ontario. Why would the opposition recommend policies that have always failed?
Look around the world and see the countries which are prosperous. They are not the ones which tolerate inflation, close their markets to trade or accumulate deficits by spending on make-work projects. This government would prefer to learn from those success stories. Why is the opposition always ready to repeat failures?

Mr. Speaker, municipalities across Canada are being hit hard by the decision of the Minister of Finance to freeze their grants in lieu of taxes at the 1992 level this year.
This drastic action will cost municipalities $40 million this year as they try to cope with rising costs for welfare and other municipal services. Other municipal taxpayers have to pay the increase in their municipal rates this year. Many of these municipal taxpayers in the Algoma riding are unemployed. Yet if they do not pay their taxes the municipality will seize their home and their property.
Why should the federal government be any different from other taxpayers? That is why this very high-handed move by the federal government places an unfair additional burden on municipalities.
I call on the Minister of Finance to reverse this decision immediately, remove the freeze on municipal grants in lieu of taxes and pay taxes just like any other taxpayer.

Mr. Speaker, a complete environmental review process was put in place with respect to the Lester B. Pearson International Airport and its expansion. The committee held extensive hearings and completed an interim report in November 1992.
The government has totally disregarded that report and has decided to build a major 8,000-foot runway 4,500 feet west of the existing north-south runway. This new runway will create a new air traffic corridor over homes, schools and the Queensway Hospital, facilities that until now have had no air noise.
The environmental review report said the buildings and homes that are seriously affected should be compensated and retrofitted with anti-noise baffling. The minister has refused to do this and refused to do anything to protect homeowners threatened by the new air corridor
March 23, 1993

and is moving in total disregard of the environmental review process.
I call on the minister and the government to change their course of action.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 20 in an article by Jane Taber in The Ottawa Citizen on the upcoming events scheduled for the Minister of National Defence it was noted that she would spend the evening at the Juno awards. Then it said: "It beats spending Sunday night in Sudbury or the North Bay legion hall wooing potential delegates".
Legion halls can be a source of much inspiration and education. Legionnaires are wonderful Canadians who care for their country. Those of us who have not participated in past conflicts can learn a lot from their experience.
As for Sudbury, it is a wonderful place in which real people have got together to overcome adversity. Chatelaine magazine included Sudbury as one of the 10 best Canadian cities to live in. Sudbury has achieved recognition for its environmental programs. The people of Sudbury have worked to diversify the economy of the area and have been and continue to be successful at it.
Unlike other levels of government Sudbury is debt free. Many would benefit from the Sudbury experience. It is a great place to visit and it is an even greater place in which to live.
The hon. member from another great place, Delta.

Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to remind the House that March is being proclaimed Help Fight Liver Disease Month by the Canadian Liver Foundation. I might add that I was going to get the member for Mississauga South to read this.
The foundation, the first organization in the world exclusively devoted to providing support for research and education on the causes of liver disease, aims to reduce the incidence and impact of all liver-related illnesses.
Among its many other services it develops support groups for the sufferers of liver disease and their families.
During the month of March the Canadian Liver Foundation's volunteer chapters will sell daisies and daisy items from booths across the country. I am sure the House will join me in congratulating the foundation on its work and in wishing it every success during Help Fight Liver Disease Month.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians are horrified by the atrocities that have been committed in the former Yugoslavia. Rape, torture and death have been inflicted on tens of thousands of women in that war-tom region.
I have in hand petitions signed by over 1,000 people in my riding calling on this government to pressure the United Nations into action. The latest reports indicate that the UN has yet to make a credible response.
Delegates to a war crimes tribunal conference have questioned the international political will to bring the perpetrators of these heinous crimes to justice.
Canadians think with honour and pride of our vaunted international peacekeeping tradition. We provide peacekeeping troops to prevent the very atrocities we know war will inevitably bring. We must now use our peacekeeping traditions to strengthen international resolve on war crimes.
I call upon the Secretary of State for External Affairs to use every effort to convince the UN to provide adequate funding for the investigation and trial of war criminals.

Mr. Speaker, recent changes to the Corrections and Conditional Release Act were intended to tighten up parole eligibility for those convicted of violent crimes. However, loopholes in the parole system are thwarting our attempts to protect the public from violent repeat offenders.

March 23, 1993
Last week Albertans learned that because of the practice of sentence merging a convict on parole who reoffends has his new sentence added to his old sentence for parole purposes. Time served on the first offence counts as time served toward parole on the second.
A convicted rapist in Edmonton sentenced to 15 years will be eligible for parole in only 18 months. If he had reoffended after his parole was completed the earliest he would have been eligible for parole would have been the year 2000.
We must ensure that the justice system works the way it is intended to, and the way Canadians expect it to. In the case of violent offenders, sentence merging for parole purposes must be stopped.

Mr. Speaker, March 21, the first day of spring for Canadians, is celebrated by Iranians throughout the world as the first day of their new year, or Nowruz, meaning new day. This secular observance of the start of the Persian calendar, the arrival of spring and the renewal of life on earth has continuously taken place over the past 2,500 years.
Iran, formerly called Persia, is one of the world's most ancient civilizations. Recent political events in that country have caused many Iranians to leave their homeland and resettle around the world, including in Canada where we have benefited much from the rich heritage of their traditions, values and ideals.
Members of this House wish a happy Nowruz to all Canadians of Iranian descent. We welcome not only their celebration of this time of renewal but also their contribution to Canada's national cultural mosaic and to our way of life.

Mr. Speaker, some of my hon. friends in opposition from the Windsor area have had nothing but ill to say of the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement since it came into effect. Perhaps I could point to some major projects in their area that
the companies involved say can be attributed in large part to an increasing flow of Canada-U.S. trade since the FTA and forecasts of even greater growth under NAFTA.
There have been $25 million in improvements to the Canadian side of the Ambassador bridge, and another $75 million on the U.S. side; $28 million will be spent upgrading the inside of the Detroit-Windsor tunnel, and another $25 million will be spent refurbishing the plaza on the Canadian side; $38 million is being spent to enlarge the CN-CP railway tunnel; a $100 million expansion of Sarnia's Blue Water bridge will be started in 1995; and there are also CN's plans for a new railway tunnel between Sarnia and Port Huron.
That is more than $290 million in investments in Canada's trade infrastructure in the Windsor-Sarnia area. Perhaps my hon. colleagues would like to comment on the jobs that investment is creating and will create in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister's recent patronage appointments to the National Parole Board have further reduced the level of corrections experience held by National Parole Board members. In fact, the percentage of board members with such experience has declined from 85 per cent in 1977 to 40 per cent today.
National Parole Board members make life and death decisions every day and as such require experience in the criminal justice field. Without such experience, their decisions may unnecessarily place Canadians at risk.
The 1988 Daubney report of the Standing Committee on Justice and the Solicitor General said:
The board can only be as good as its decision makers. If those who are appointed as decision makers do not have the requisite qualifications or experience, their decision making is unlikely to be as effective as it should be.
I call upon the Prime Minister and the Solicitor General to re-examine the process of making these appointments and to put the safety of Canadians first instead of delivering million dollar farewell gifts to Tory supporters.
March 23, 1993

Mr. Speaker, Olympic gold medalists Kerrin Lee-Gartner and Mark Tewksbury were chosen outstanding Canadian athletes by the Sports Federation of Canada last night. Lee-Gartner of Calgary won the Velma Springstead award as Canada's female athlete of the year. Tewksbury, also of Calgary, took home the Norman H. Crowe Award as the top male athlete.
Several other Canadian athletes were also honoured at the federation's annual awards banquet. The gold medal winning women's eight rowing team from Barcelona was team of the year. Nicolas Gill of Montreal won the Viscount Alexander award as top junior male athlete. Nancy Drolet of Drummondville won the Elaine Tanner award as the top junior female athlete.
A friend and colleague, Alwin Morris, was also awarded the Johnny F. Bassett award for exemplary community service, a recognition for all his work in developing indigenous sports programs helping youth across Canada.
I ask the House to join me in congratulating all these outstanding Canadians, athletes who in their own special way have always made us proud to be Canadian, and the Sports Federation of Canada for its work and recognition.

Mr. Speaker, unfortunately the provincial government in Manitoba is planning to continue with its proposed Assiniboine River water diversion.
According to the Supreme Court ruling on the Oldman Dam case in January 1992, the federal government may do an environmental review when there is an affirmative regulatory power involved. The Minister of the Environment confirmed his acceptance of this view when I asked him about this in May 1992.
The fact that federal funding for this water diversion comes from the western diversification fund and the prairie farm rehabilitation administration, that the Assiniboine is a navigable river, that aboriginal land will be
Oral Questions
affected, and that irrigation in one region is being favoured over potable use in another, gives the federal government plenty of jurisdiction and responsibility for a proper assessment.
A basin-wide review is necessary to study the cumulative effect of this development. There will be a reduction in the amount of water and an increase in the concentration of chemical pollutants already in the river from agricultural run-off and industry, namely from the American based pharmaceutical company, Ayerst.
I call on the Minister of the Environment to live up to the image he is fond of projecting in his leadership campaign and order the assessment.

['I listened very carefully to the exchange between the hon. member and the minister. The hon. member is rising now and seeks some information with respect to jurisdiction in this matter.
First of all, it is not for the Chair to enter into that debate. I say this with respect, but nonetheless I remind the hon. member that in a very real sense he is extending the debate which arose with the questions and answers.
The hon. member, of course, has the right to ask questions of the appropriate nominated member of the Board of Internal Economy if he wishes to do so. If that is the route he wishes to follow, then I am sure with consultation he could find an appropriate time to put a question of that sort.
It is certainly not for the Chair to get into an argument about where the jurisdiction is in this particular case.']

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask a question of the Prime Minister.
We know that President Yeltsin has not yet asked for a change of venue for the meeting in Vancouver in 10 days, but today the Deputy Prime Minister of Russia said: "We will prepare this meeting to take place in Moscow. This will be a symbol of support for our country".
In light of the statement of the Deputy Prime Minister of Russia, will the Canadian government indicate that Canada will not be offended at all if the United States and Russia were to move the venue to Moscow?

Mr. Speaker, I indicated yesterday that we would not in any way be offended at all if the venue were moved anywhere that would benefit the bilateral arrangements and the support for President Yeltsin and his democratic reform.
We are happy to make all the arrangements to accommodate both parties in Vancouver. Should either or both decide that it could best be held and more advantageously be held for President Yeltsin elsewhere, we would be happy to accommodate that.

March 23, 1993
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary for the Prime Minister.
Yesterday in Chicago the U.S. Secretary of State argued in favour of an aid package that would be better targeted and better co-ordinated by western countries. Mr. Christopher also said that to achieve this a meeting of Group of Seven finance ministers and foreign affairs ministers should be held as soon as possible.
Would the Prime Minister agree that this meeting should preferably be held before the meeting between President Yeltsin and President Clinton, and that it would be advisable to try and organize a meeting early next week to pave the way for the meeting scheduled between the two presidents in Vancouver or Moscow?

Mr. Speaker, I am aware of what was said by Mr. Christopher yesterday in Chicago.
Perhaps I may point out to the Leader of the Opposition that on May 21 last year I said the following at John Hopkins University in Baltimore, and I quote: "I believe that so far the west's collective response has been hesitant and timid and certainly not commensurate with the needs and opportunities that are out there". I was referring to a collective response by the west to the problems of President Yeltsin and to opportunities in the former Soviet Union. That was my government's position a year and a half or two years ago, and it still is today.
In fact, earlier today I received a call from President Frangois Mitterand of France who shared this opinion and who believes, as I do, that the problem is a complex one and that if there is a change of plan with respect to a bilateral meeting, it may be useful for G-7 members to consider a meeting of heads of government or heads of State. The problem is so important and so complex that it requires political leadership by heads of government. That is President Mitterand's position and it is also the position of the Canadian government.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Prime Minister.
I would like to know from the Prime Minister if it is the intention of the Canadian government to make sure that there will be a linkage between the aid packages and the maintenance of a democratically elected government in Russia.
We would like to know if the aid will be linked to democracy or separated. It is very important to know so that there will be pressure on the people in Russia to make sure that they maintain a democratically elected government in that country.

Mr. Speaker, the link must be direct, evident and ongoing. In the same speech at Johns Hopkins University at the commencement exercises on May 21, 1992 I indicated that it was time to unite the people of the former Soviet Union with democrats everywhere.
The first step is to complete the integration of the countries of the former Soviet Union into the global economic system. This refers to IMF, World Bank membership, the creation of stabilization funds, individual technical assistance programs, and the coming together of the G-7 with a view to dealing with this fundamental problem.
My friend and I have discussed in the past how much Canada, the United States and other G-7 countries would have paid had the leader of the Soviet Union said 15 years ago: "I am ready to get out to disband the Warsaw pact. We are going to facilitate the unification of Germany. We are going to bring about a democratic system in Russia and the Soviet Union and end the cold war".
What would the G-7 countries have been ready to say at the time? They would have said: "How much can we provide, when and where?"
The absence of this kind of response is why I said at Johns Hopkins that the western collective approach thus far had been timid and lacking in daring and responsibility. I think the time has come, even at this late hour, for us to respond in the manner suggested by my hon. friend with a profound linkage to democratic institutions and democracy itself in Russia as best exemplified by the
March 23, 1993

maintenance of President Yeltsin in office as the only elected head of government in Russia in a thousand years.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister.
It was reported in The Winnipeg Free Press today that the Minister of Agriculture indicated that the government is considering spending an extra $80 million to make up the shortfall of 500,000 tonnes of grain promised or committed to Russia last June.
Is the government simply going to unfreeze the credit system that was arrived at last June? Are we planning to spend an extra $80 million to fulfil the previous commitment? Or, are there going to be new commitments made for new grain assistance to Russia?
If I might ask as well, is the government considering altering the charter or the legislation of the Wheat Board to allow it to engage in direct barter arrangements with Russia in order to facilitate the grain trade between the two countries?

Mr. Speaker, in regard to the question raised by my hon. friend, 523,000 tonnes out of 1 million tonnes of the grain shipment agreed to in June have already been shipped. Shipments were temporarily suspended simply because Russia was paying some creditors in hard cash and not honouring some commitments to Canada.
Had all of us been placed on the same footing there would have been no difficulty. But I have had discussions with President Yeltsin about this. The matter is satisfactorily resolved and our expectation is we will be able to proceed.
I mention as well the question properly raised by my friend yesterday about the nuclear safety initiative, which was a $30 million commitment by Canada over three years. Approximately $8 million will be disbursed in this fiscal year honouring that commitment.
Technical assistance in general, which is a very vast and I think constructive program between Canada and Russia with a wide range of projects, is well under way in some pretty impressive people-to-people ways. I give my hon. friend one illustration: 700 Russian oilfield workers and managers are being trained as a result of Canadian assistance in safety and petroleum production. With the
Oral Questions
assistance of Canadian community colleges funded by Canada the training programs at three Russian oil and gas institutes are being significantly upgraded with 20,000 Russian students benefiting from Canadian expertise delivered at the ground floor level.
If we multiply this kind of technical assistance program perhaps dozens of times we get an indication of what Canada has been seeking to do.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister was quoted yesterday as saying that they are now looking at another aid package that might be part of a larger commitment, and I think he indicated there have been some initial discussions.
Given that Canadians share this deep concern about the seriousness of the situation in Russia, but also knowing that we live very much in a time of constraint, I think it is clear that any new initiative should have the support of the public as expressed in this Parliament.
I want to ask the Prime Minister if the government would commit to full parliamentary consultations on any new aid or assistance package so there can be a consensus on what Canada can do to assist the people of Russia, so we can determine where the money will come from and what purposes will be served.
The Prime Minister would agree it is important at this time to have full agreement and consent of the people of this country as expressed through all their parliamentary representatives.

Mr. Speaker, I certainly agree with the suggestion of my hon. friend that a parliamentary debate on this matter would be very appropriate. Obviously the government would be happy to lay its plan in this regard on the floor of the House of Commons. My hon. friend can comment on it, approve it, criticize it and do all the things we ought to do in a parliament.
When one looks back at the Marshall plan and the extraordinary success it had in rebuilding Europe and in maintaining vibrant democracies throughout European countries that had once been devastated, when one considers the extremely modest contributions, relatively speaking, being sought for the former Soviet Union and the timidity and the hesitation encountered in some G-7 and other industrialized countries, it is astonishing to see that this is actually taking place.

March 23, 1993
Oral Questions
It is time for the leaders of the world in respect of this great challenge to stop thinking like bookkeepers and to think like statesmen and visionaries because that is what is required in regard to the former Soviet Union and democracy in Russia.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance.
The Governor of the Bank of Canada today put forward his sixth annual report wherein he said, not surprisingly, that debt reduction should be an important priority.
I want to say to the Minister of Finance that this is the same Governor of the Bank of Canada who raised the interest rates in order to control inflation. For every point those interest rates were raised $1.5 billion was added to the debt and that high interest rate policy created record bankruptcies among farms, individuals and businesses. It is the same Governor of the Bank of Canada who deliberately created unemployment in Canada.
I want to ask the Minister of Finance if he is not shocked that the Governor of the Bank of Canada does not see the failure of these policies after six years and bring out a new directive. If not, will he bring in the Governor of the Bank of Canada and tell him it will be impossible to address the debt in this country as long as that governor supports 1.5 million unemployed in this country?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am shocked at the rationale that the hon. leader of the NDP is using.
I think she is a supporter of lower interest rates in this country. In order to have low interest rates you have to have low inflation. That is why we have today the lowest bank rate in 21 years and the lowest mortgages in 35 years. Why is the hon. member opposed to that?
I think the hon. member also recognizes that we have to get the fundamentals right. Today's Ottawa Citizen
says: "Economic recovery ready to roll". Another headline says: "Recovery posts steady gain, analysts say".
You have been trying for eight years.
It is 10 points down today.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: There we go again. No one likes good news over on that side of the House. Well, the news is improving, employment is improving, growth of the economy is improving, exports are improving, utilization is improving, housing sales are up and manufacturing sales are up. Why is the hon. member arguing with those results?

A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker.
It is clear that if this government and the Governor of the Bank of Canada had not had the kind of fiscal and monetary policy that has been in place in the last six years and had this government not doubled the debt in the last eight and a half years, we would not need these measures for the recovery that he is talking about. We would not need to have a bigger recovery because we would not have had as big a problem.
It is clear that this government and the Governor of the Bank of Canada had implemented for a number of years a monetary policy which led to a made-in-Canada recession. Two economic analysts both respected in Canada, Informetrica and WEFA, have indicated that we would have higher employment and a greater gross domestic product if interest rates had been kept lower at that time.
I say to the minister that it is his government's policies, supported by the Governor of the Bank of Canada, that created the problems. Will he bring in a budget to address the problem because the problem is the unemployment created by this government?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. leader of the New Democratic Party should get together with the premiers of the provinces of Ontario, Saskatchewan and British Columbia who recognize that deficits and debts are a serious problem in this country.
If she wants to talk about records in accumulating debts, I remind the hon. member that under the Liberal government the debt multiplied 11 times.
March 23, 1993

Quite frankly, as The Toronto Star pointed out: "The seeds of disaster were planted in 1975". That just so happens to follow that marriage of convenience that took place between the Liberals and the NDP between 1972 and 1974.

Mr. Speaker, no province ever signed a free trade agreement that cost the country more than 100,000 jobs, and no province created the excessively high interest rates that led to a record number of bankruptcies in this country.
I have a question for the minister. This country does not want any advice about the debt. What this country needs is specific steps to create jobs. How can the minister expect us to consider the debt problem when we have about 1.5 million unemployed in this country? How can we, with an unemployment rate of nearly 11 per cent?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is rather amusing. I find it strange that the hon. leader of the New Democratic Party would criticize policies like the free trade agreement and policies like the GST which are really the instruments that are driving the economy out of recession.
It is exports that are driving the economy. I know the hon. member does not believe in liberalized free trade. She believes we can build a wall around Canada and trade our way to prosperity. That is not the way we feel about it. The fact of the matter is the trading initiatives, thanks in large part to the free trade agreement, and in large part the contribution of the GST in improving the competitiveness and productivity are the two most important features which are driving this economy out of recession.

Mr. Speaker, a number of trade experts from the C.D. Howe Institute to the government's own recent prosperity initiative have identified as the central weakness of the North American free trade agreement the continuing absence of a
Oral Questions
common set of trading rules. Yet the minister has said that Canada cannot propose a parallel accord on such common trade rules in the current negotiations with Canada and Mexico because, and I quote: "Any change in the subsidies code would entail reopening the agreement".
Why does Canada not propose a parallel accord on subsidies? Can the minister explain why a parallel accord on subsidies proposed by Canada would entail reopening the North American free trade agreement while parallel accords on the environment and labour proposed by the United States do not reopen the agreement?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, trade rules are at the heart and core of a free trade agreement. Rules related to the environment or labour matters are not at the core of a free trade agreement. If you want to have changes in the rules on the subsidies or countervail or anti-dumping, you have to reopen the agreement. That is logical.
If my hon. friend says he wants to reopen the agreement, what is he prepared to give up? What is he prepared to change? The Americans are seeking changes in the cultural exemption. They are seeking changes in the supply management system. The members of Congress are seeking changes in the dispute settlement mechanism. Those are the three priorities that the Americans want. Which one of those would my hon. friend give up in return for changes in the subsidies code?

Mr. Speaker, the minister says that parallel accords on the environment and on labour standards are virtually meaningless. Let us be clear on this. He says that they are not central to the agreement, but that a subsidies code, which we do not have and he has never negotiated, is central to the agreement but he cannot get it.
If Canada cannot propose a parallel accord on subsidies, on common trading rules, the least the minister can do in the negotiations which resume next month is to propose a trinational panel to work out a common set of trade rules. How can Mexico and the United States refuse to participate in such a panel? Why does he not take that initiative to represent Canadian interests?

March 23, 1993
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, let us just make sure that my hon. friend and I are on the same wavelength here.
We both agree that the subsidies code is in the agreement. There is a subsidies code in the agreement. My hon. friend is nodding. He would like to see some improvements in that. I also would like to see improvements in that but we have to get agreement.
Where we do have agreement is in the GATT. The proposals that have been made by Director General Dunkel on the subsidies code are very acceptable to Canada. We have participated fully in the negotiations there and that, I think, would answer the questions that my hon. friend has. I would encourage him to be somewhat patient. He will get a Uruguay round and he will get the subsidies code.

Mr. Speaker, my question is also to the Minister for International Trade.
Today in Washington, over 600 representatives of the American lumber and home-building industry are asking President Clinton and Congress to repeal the 6.5 per cent tax on softwood lumber.
This tax not only increases the cost of a home in the United States by over 4 per cent but it hurts every Canadian softwood producer and hurts every Canadian worker.
Will the minister ask the President directly to repeal this tax at the April 2 timber summit that is being held in Portland, Oregon?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 11 will be meeting with the U.S. trade representative Mr. Mickey Kantor. I will be raising the matter of the softwood lumber issue at that time.
I know my hon. friend realizes there is a process that must be gone through. We must respect that process on both sides. I know that he has heard me say many times in the House that there was no basis on which the softwood lumber issue should have been brought to a countervailing duty position.
The government has taken a very strong position on that. In fact what we have been doing since that time is
engaging in an advocacy exercise in the United States where we have gone to the home builders in the United States. I believe that our efforts have been instrumental in part in the positions that these home builders have taken and that he just referred to.

Mr. Speaker, a supplementary question to the same minister and on the same issue.
We both realize that the softwood lumber industry can be the one bright spot on the Canadian resource horizon if this government ensures that sufficient assistance is given to all of these areas.
I know that in my area alone we could create 1,000 new jobs almost immediately. Will this government make loan guarantees and other resources available to all of the sawmill operators throughout Canada so they can modernize and better compete in this vital industry that is absolutely hot? This government should be taking advantage of it today.

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend thinks he has put all the facts, but I believe that it is not possible in Question Period. Let me draw a couple of others.
There has been almost a doubling in the price of lumber in the last year or so. There has also been a drop in the value of the Canadian dollar so that the returns to the lumber producers in Canada, including in his constituency, have increased significantly in recent months. They now have the cash flow and can do some of the expansions that he is looking for.
That together with the changes in the Small Businesses Loans Act that my friend the Minister of Finance has brought in, plus the drop in interest rates that has resulted from the drop in inflation, all combine to put in place an environment which is very very positive for investment in that industry.

subtopic: PARLIAMENTARY EMPLOYMENT AND STAFF RELATIONS ACT
PARLIAMENTARY EMPLOYMENT AND STAFF RELATIONS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the President of the Privy Council. In his absence, perhaps the government House leader can deal with it.
March 23, 1993

Oral Questions
Six and three-quarter years ago in June 1986, the 33rd Parliament, with all-party support, passed the government's Bill C-45 and enacted the Parliamentary Employment and Staff Relations Act, which very simply extended to workers on Parliament Hill the same basic rights to decent working conditions and health and safety laws enjoyed by all other federal employees.
Almost seven years and one election has passed since Royal Assent was given. Still the cabinet has not proclaimed the operative sections of the act, parts II and III, into law. My question is: Will the government proclaim this important basic legislation before the end of this Parliament? Just when will it act to end this obvious and continuing injustice to those who serve us in this place?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: PARLIAMENTARY EMPLOYMENT AND STAFF RELATIONS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the government, we say that it is not really the government that is holding up this issue. This issue deals exclusively with the House of Commons, with employees of the House of Commons and with employees of individual members.
There are certain aspects of the law which would impose on individual members some requirements that there has been some reluctance to take on. The proper forum to discuss this is the Board of Internal Economy. I will certainly relay the hon. member's concerns to the board.

subtopic: PARLIAMENTARY EMPLOYMENT AND STAFF RELATIONS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after seven years, I and I am sure the workers of Parliament find that answer absolutely up on cloud nine.
The workers we are talking about not only work directly for members of Parliament but they are all of those employees, some unionized some not, who are employed here for the House of Commons, whether they are security workers, whether they carry out the garbage, whether they cook in the kitchens or whatever else. Surely if there was to be a consultation process, they and any Canadians-who I must admit expect the wheels of government to grind slowly, especially this government's-have a right to expect that it will be less than seven years before consultations are held and something gets done. It is an obvious injustice.
Why has the government not acted at this time? What is the reason? Did it not know what it was doing or does it not know what it is doing now?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: PARLIAMENTARY EMPLOYMENT AND STAFF RELATIONS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps the hon. member was rehearsing his supplementary question and did not hear my first answer.
This is not a government question. It is a House of Commons question. There is a distinction. The Board of Internal Economy has the responsibility for this and the hon. member's party has a representative on the Board of Internal Economy. If there was such indignation in the NDP caucus all these years, how come it was never raised by the hon. member's representative?

Mr. Speaker, last December, the Minister of Transport promised in the House that he would present a plan in early February to stabilize the airline industry. Today is March 23, and since Canadian International and Air Canada had huge losses in 1992 and Nationair now needs protection from its creditors, is the minister finally prepared to announce measures to stabilize an airline industry that is on the brink?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member opposite will surely recall that I informed the House in November that if the airlines did not impose the self-discipline required to return to profitability, we would intervene by proposing corrective measures in this House.
Since then, the two airlines have announced reductions in their capacity that are likely to improve their situation. We are continuing to examine various options available to correct the situation if the airlines do not continue in the same direction.

Mr. Speaker, the airline industry has a lot of high quality, high paying jobs that are clearly in jeopardy. It now seems clear that the

March 23, 1993
Oral Questions
basis of the minister's policy is that airline companies will fail.
Will the minister disclose to the House what he expects will be the total loss of employment in the airline industry when his policies have had their full effect?

Mr Speaker, I do not believe the member is suggesting that the Government of Canada should manage the two national airlines. The representatives of these two airlines have said repeatedly over the past few weeks that overcapacity is their main problem.
As far as I am concerned, they control the capacity and can address the problem themselves if they want their industry to survive.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. He will know that Canadians are massively opposed to the purchase of the EH-101 helicopter for the sum of some $5.8 billion at a time when one million children live in poverty and 700,000 children use food banks.
I want to know from the Minister of Finance if he personally supported the purchase of the helicopters. Yes or no?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Dick (Minister of Supply and Services):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member knows, the government made a decision in 1987 to purchase the EH-101. It confirmed and signed a contract in October 1992. The government stands behind that decision.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is interesting to note that the Minister of Finance did not defend the helicopter purchase.
I want to ask a supplementary question of the Minister of Finance.

The helicopters cost $5.8 billion. Some manufacturers are bankrupt and Canadians have had enough of this whole affair.
So I come back to the Minister of Finance. Is he prepared to tell us today whether or not he still supports buying these helicopters at a cost of $5.8 billion? This is a simple question.

Mr. Speaker, a simple answer for a simple question.
The Canadian government has made a decision in the national interest and in the interest of our Armed Forces and our UN peacekeeping forces. We need this equipment and we will acquire these helicopters with a 13-year program, instead of having 30, 40 or 50-year old helicopters that could endanger the lives and safety of our soldiers and those who have the heavy responsibility of defending Canada's interests.

My friend asks whether one minister is supporting this. Well, of course, all the ministers are supporting it. Only in the Liberal Party does the leader go one way and the party the other.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the minister of immigration. First I would like to congratulate him for adopting new guidelines for women refugees facing gender discrimination.
Based on these guidelines I would ask the minister if he will review the case of my constituent, Amina Mohamed, who along with her four sons is to be deported tomorrow to the U.S. and then to Somalia. As a divorced Muslim woman, she has no status and will be shunned. Her parents are dead and she faces grave danger.
Will the minister delay the departure of this woman and her sons and personally review her case based on the new gender discrimination guidelines?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, because of the Privacy Act I cannot discuss any particular case in the House of Commons. But I can undertake to review the case the hon. member mentions.

I want to thank the minister. I want to mention also that we have an affidavit from American lawyers which proves that if
March 23, 1993

she is deported to the United States she will be ineligible for refugee status and will be deported from there.
I would ask the minister also to look at this case from a compassionate point of view, to allow this family to remain in Canada where the woman has support from her family and friends-
The question is becoming a brief on behalf of the lady. I understand that but it is going too far. Does the minister wish to respond?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, all I can assure the hon. member is that I shall be reviewing the particular case she has mentioned and will get back to her for further details or information she may have.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
The report of the UN truth commission on El Salvador both names and condemns those on both sides who committed heinous atrocities during the war years and attempts to contribute to reconciliation by recommending inter alia that all of the persons named be barred from public office. Yet last Saturday, almost before the ink on the report was dry, President Cristiani moved to grant amnesty to all those named, including apparently those already convicted and in jail for the infamous murder of the Jesuit priests.
Will the minister undertake to convey to President Cristiani that many Canadians who care about the peace process and who have seen him exercise constructive leadership in the past feel betrayed by this action? Will Canada urge him to implement the recommendations of the report in full?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yes we will do that directly with the president. Through my colleague, the Minister for External Relations, we have conveyed that directly to El Salvador's minister for economic and social development.
We will take every avenue in which to do this. We think it is a cynical use of the amnesty procedure, given the need of El Salvador to continue down the track of economic and democratic reform which we have strongly
Oral Questions
supported. We have strongly supported the President when he has made those moves. We will be equally strong in condemning him as a result of this very cynical action.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for my friend, the minister of fisheries.
He will know that today in Halifax fishermen in large numbers are there to send a strong message to him and the government for the way they have handled the fisheries crisis, as did hundreds of fishermen in Sydney yesterday. They are there for very good reason. It is because the government has failed to provide a compensation package for those people who have been victimized by the severe quota cuts and the downturn in catches.
The government is putting the blocks to fishermen on the licence issue and it has the industry in a spin over its cock-eyed reform proposals.
Why is it that the minister insists on putting the boots to these people whom he should be helping?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that all members can recognize the partisan and silly nature of that question because the record speaks for itself.
Whenever fishermen have needed to be assisted by this government they have been assisted. That goes from ice compensation, when there was an unusual ice condition several years ago; to a gear up program, to help them when they needed assistance in gearing up after having a bad year; to the Atlantic Fisheries Adjustment Program, $584 million; to the northern cod program, $780 million.
With respect to licensing and the new Atlantic ground-fish management plan and reform of the department of fisheries, there is widespread support across the country except in Newfoundland. You can never expect any support from that government for anything constructive. So we have no support from that particular government which does nothing but criticize and condemn-

Oral Questions

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I thought you liked Clyde Wells.
Let us try to move on.

Okay, okay, I will tell Clyde you still love him.
Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is for the same minister. I want to ask the minister again, if things are as hunky-dory and as perfect as he suggested in his answer a moment ago, what is it about ail those hundreds and thousands of people in Halifax yesterday and Sydney today? Is it that in his army everybody is out of step except him? Is that the problem, that he is the perfect guy and these people are all wet? Or maybe they have a cause.
Would the minister recognize that and agree now to do something about their concerns instead of ballyhooing as he is doing here today?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Fisheries and Oceans

subtopic: GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES RESTRAINT ACT, 1993 NO. 2 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to debate the issue this afternoon on Bill C-113 at the report stage. This is the bill, as you know, for government expenditures.
The bill is a fairly complex one, comprised of four parts. I am going to address that part concerned with unemployment insurance because it is the most controversial part of the bill and has received most of the attention in both the media and the public eye. Perhaps more specifically and more important, it has received the most scrutiny and concern from those many unemployed Canadians who are now desperate and in the ranks of
over 1.5 million Canadians, on the issues that are being debated.
It bothers me and a lot of my constituents that in its mini budget of December 3 last the government did not come up with measures and macro-measures to put some of the unemployed back to work and save money on the deficit.
Instead it is trying to save $2.35 billion by attacking those people who need to be attacked least. It is reducing the benefits for the unemployed from 60 to 57 per cent and imposing what I believe are unfair penalties on those people who quite often, through no fault of their own, have to quit their jobs and go to work elsewhere.
There is nobody in this House who needs to be told what the unemployment insurance program is all about, but there are some changes that have been made since this group of politicians was elected in 1988. Considerable changes were made to the program that I suppose in part are responsible for this shameful measure that is being debated in the House today.
The unemployment insurance program is the federal government's largest single expenditure and exceeds national defence costs, Old Age Security costs and the total administration costs of the federal government. Its forecasted cost for 1993 is $22.5 billion.
I think the key issue here, and it has not been missed by some speakers, is the fact that until 1990 when Bill C-21 was passed, the government paid up to 26 per cent of the unemployment insurance fund. That does not happen any more. The unemployment insurance fund is now totally paid for by employers and employees. Essentially it is a private insurance fund.
I do not believe the money that will be lost by those people who are involved in pursuing their claims from 60 per cent to 57 per cent is going to be equivalent to the difficulties people will have who quit their jobs through no fault of their own. Irrespective of the changes that were made since Bill C-105, which was so unpopular it had to be changed, those people are being asked now to go to appeal. I believe it is tantamount to telling them they are guilty and have to prove themselves innocent. It
March 23, 1993

is all very well to say they can appeal, but what does that mean?
In 1991, 191,000 UI applicants were held to have quit their jobs and were penalized. About 10 per cent or
19,000	of these decisions were reversed by various boards. As you know, we have 99 boards of appeal that include roughly 1,000 people. Canada has 450 CEC centres, but about 250 of them actually process claims. If we look at the volume of information that is involved, last year in the 29 telecentres, 8.65 million telephone calls were made on the subject of these appeals to sort out clarifications in the unemployment insurance decisions made by follow-on appeals, boards and eventually judges.
If that was worked out on the back of a cigarette package, 8.65 million telephone calls in a year at 29 centres with an average number of working days in the year, it works out to 1,300 to 1,500 calls a day. This bill tells people: "Do not worry, you are going to be guilty". In other words, it is assumed you have quit for reasons that would penalize you. If you think you have a case, come back and see us with the 1,900 other appellants, the 1,500 phone calls a day and the 250 centres across Canada.
My confidence in that is not very strong and I will tell you why. I just recently learned of a case. Reference was made to it today by the hon. member for Port Moody- Coquitlam, but not in the context I am going to report to the House. It will give some indication of the confusion and difficulty one has in actually appealing a case. This case does not even relate to an appeal. I am not going to use names because I think there will be less of a bias.
I am reporting information that was given to me on March 18. It involved a lady in one part of Canada. She was planning to quit a job she had for almost 15 years to join her fiance who was posted to another part of Canada. She had to resign because she was obviously moving to another place. Before she made this decision she contacted the UI office in her area and asked if she could collect benefits if she were to quit her job and follow her fiance. After looking at the circumstances involved, the answer from the office was yes.
She made the move and later expected to receive her benefits. After some inquiries she received two letters
Government Orders
on the same day at her new address from the Unemployment Insurance Commission. One said she was entitled to the claim she had filed. The other letter from the same office said she had been disqualified from receiving benefits for seven weeks because she had quit her job voluntarily without just cause. This letter said her benefit rate would also be reduced. The point I am making here is that one letter recognized the relationship she was having with her fiance as a common-law relationship. The other did not because it was reckoned they had not been living together full time for a year. The letters were from the same office, dated the same day and more remarkably were from the same person.
How in the name of Heaven can we expect a member of Parliament, who has been invited to participate in this process by the latest circulars being passed out to employees and the public, to get a handle on a system of flexibility and judgment that allows one person to give two completely opposite answers to the same person in one day? It is bad enough to give one answer with identical circumstances to two different people. It does not excuse the poor judgment made there. But to actually send it to the same person and presumably not know it was going to the same person indicates the kind of system we are being asked to cope with if we pass this legislation.
There is a great belief that those people who quit their jobs go away and never look for work and are a total drain on the work force of Canada. The facts do not support that.
An analysis of the unemployment figures done in 1986 showed that half of all job quitters went to another job immediately. I believe the premise that is inherent in this bill has been the basis of all the vindictive discussion that is going on. The reason the government is having a lot of trouble with this bill, even in its own party, is because it has not really done its homework. Also, it is trying to save money and cut the deficit by nickel and diming and hitting those people who can least afford it.
I believe that is probably one of the most despicable things this government has done in the eight and a half years it has been in power. I for one, and I believe I am speaking for my party, will not be voting to support these measures.

March 23, 1993
Government Orders

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just want to make a few comments before I launch into my main burden about the comments made by my predecessor. Although I agree essentially with his remarks, I think he has been misled into believing this is an attempt to save money. When he says nickels and dimes, that is part of the trap the government is trying to create.
This bill really has more to do with the harmonization required under the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement and the North American free trade agreement with Mexico. I will take my friend through this step by step so he will recognize how insidious this bill is. Not only is it an attack on the unemployed, it is a capitulation to the loss of sovereignty of the nation of Canada to determine its own policies because of the signing of the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement.
I know when I am through there will be one Liberal in this House who will stand with me when we fight the NAFTA deal and demand the abrogation of the free trade agreement. It is regrettable that the Liberal Party has abandoned its position on this issue and its trade critic has accepted NAFTA with some fancy petticoats, but it is essentially the same agreement, an extension of loss of sovereignty. When I am through speaking I know that good member will support me as the lone Liberal in this House against this particular bill.
Mr. Speaker, I know it comes to your edification that this is the second step in destroying the unemployment insurance program as we have known it in this country since we signed the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement.
The United States signatories to the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement have insisted all along that our unemployment insurance benefits are far too beneficial to the recipients compared to the Americans.
The first assault on the Canadian unemployment insurance program, in terms of harmonization and a level playing field, was the de Grandpre report, which was tabled in this House as promised by this government to make sure that workers would allegedly be protected from the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement fall-out.
Almost every major recommendation of the government's own de Grandpre report was ignored. It went in the opposite direction. The first thing it did three years
ago was to slash the amount of weeks that a beneficiary could receive the insurance that he or she bought.
It was the first step on the road to harmonization. This unemployment insurance bill that we are dealing with now is the second chapter delivered from Washington, D.C., through the Tory government.
This is harmonization number two, and if the government keeps it up it will sell it as a video tape. It could call it "Terminator One of UIC" and now "Terminator Two of UIC". It is all written in the United States of America in Washington, D.C.
Does anyone think this government is standing up and fighting for Canadian working men and women? Mr. Speaker, I know that you cannot say because you are in the chair, but if you could speak I know you would agree with what I am saying and say that this government is heading on a sinful path.
I would further say that this government had lied to the Canadian people, but accusing the government of lying is out of order and the last thing I would do is break the rules of this House by accusing the government of lying.
Maybe some of its candidates did, and that is what bothers me. The impression was left with the Canadian people that the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement would be a harmonization that would bring American standards up to Canadian, and then NAFTA would be a harmonization bringing Mexican standards up to Canadian. Nothing could be further from truth. Every single step is a cutback and a cut down to the American standards and ultimately to Mexican standards.
Some wag suggested that the Minister of Finance would end up, as a result of the NAFTA agreement and this kind of legislation, no longer selling used cars but used tacos. That is the kind of harmonization we are moving toward. Everything that is the lowest common denominator in these agreements between Canada, the United States and Mexico is the direction in which we are going.
Who is standing up and fighting for the unemployed in this country? Not the government, not the Liberal opposition. It is regrettable that both the government and the Liberal opposition have been captivated by this same course of cutting the services in this country to meet the new global economy as defined by the United States.
March 23, 1993

This bill written in Washington, D.C. and sent up, I hope with adequate postage, to this government is an example of the kind of harmonization that is destroying the social fabric of the Canadian work place.
Why would a government move in this direction at this time unless harmonization was the goal? What the government does not talk about is the growing banking system for the poor. One of the fastest growing banking systems for the poor are the food banks. We now have more food banks in this country than we have McDonald's restaurants. Two million people a week are lining up at food banks in this country. That is a record of the Tory government, the free trade agreement and harmonization.
There are 1.5 million people unemployed and the number is rising. Instead of giving people an option to have more time to find ways of finding a job the government is cutting back on access to unemployment insurance and on the payments themselves.
It seems obvious that this government has abandoned its responsibility to Canadians, except for Canadian industries that are a pale reflection of the corporate agenda dictated by the United States and the international capital community.
It does not like to hear these words any more. It believes that the new global economy demands that we cut the guts out of everything we have fought for in this country on behalf of working men and working women. It is urging workers to be more productive with less wages. It is urging men and women to not dare to give up their jobs, even if they are harassed or the working conditions are subhuman, because they will be punished under this bill if they do so.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, two minutes. I thought for a moment that you were giving me a salutary greeting but I understand it was just the two-minute signal. Nonetheless, I appreciate your friendliness.
It is unbelievable that this House is not jam-packed for every second of this debate because this debate is at the crux of the social fabric of which this nation is built and which is being abandoned by the Conservative government at the behest of its erstwhile partners in the American business community who are dictating the policy for the Canadian nation.

This bill is an example, quietly and relentlessly pushing its way through this House, of how the Tories have capitulated to outside capital interests to destroy a competitive edge we had in terms of Canadian working men and women.
What is furthermore regrettable is that while image is being pursued by the mass media around the Tory leadership candidates, not one of them has been asked whether or not he or she will vote against this bill to show that they are different than the present Prime Minister of this country.
They can change a man's suit or a woman's hair-do but that does not change that person's policy. It does not matter a fig who is leading that party over there because they support this kind of legislation which hurts Canadian working men and women.
My dear friend across is mumbling but I do not interpret those mumbles other than as a subdued confession that he, too, will abandon the possibility of running for office simply out of shame at what this bill is doing.
I know that my time is up in this debate, but I want to warn the government that I will be relentless in my pursuit of the fact that none of the leadership candidates of the Conservative Party has taken any position other than to support this destruction of unemployment insurance as we know it. Let every woman and man in this country know exactly what the government is doing.

March 23, 1993
Government Orders
When this piece of legislation came forward I was trying to figure out where it was coming from.
When I returned to my constituency office, about one week or so after the first session that we had on this bill and after parts of it were introduced during the economic statement, the people that supported this bill in my community were the people who seemed to be doing okay in terms of their own jobs. For starters, I must say there were very few. They would say: "The government is really doing a good job of cleaning up the abuse".
I reflected for a while and I said that now we know the genesis of where this bill is coming from. This bill was designed to try to send a signal to Canadians that in the name of efficiency the government was going to clean up the Unemployment Insurance Act.
It is a cruel piece of legislation when we have an economy in which 1.6 million people are on the unemployment insurance rolls. The latest Statistics Canada numbers show us that 2.2 million people are on the welfare rolls in this country. This piece of legislation does nothing for the people who are out of work.
It does absolutely nothing for the dignity of people who are in tenuous situations in companies. We have already discussed at length the situations that can exist in companies in terms of harassment being a cause for someone to want to leave, and we have discussed how they are not protected under this bill as clearly as they should be.
This bill was packaged, created and put here to appeal to the right wing in this country. Everything now is done in the name of deficit and debt reduction. Those who are most disadvantaged in our community seem to be on the short end of the stick.
The government has missed the whole point of why it is here. Governments are not here for the advantaged. It is not here just to develop policy for the advantaged. first premise of why we are in government. It does not meet the test of looking after those who are disadvantaged.
I stand here today in total opposition to this bill. We in the Liberal Party are not against cleaning up any abuse in the system. We do not tolerate people who are trying to take advantage of the system.

Instead of spending all of this time trying to focus on the abuse factor, which the government has said costs somewhere in the neighbourhood of $200 million out of the close to $35 billion that was paid out last year in unemployment insurance and welfare, and taking all this time to restructure the Unemployment Insurance Act so dramatically in the name of that $200 million, this government should be creating hope and designing policies that will spark or ignite small business people in this country so that they can put people back to work.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in the House this afternoon to speak to Bill C-113, because according to me and according to my colleague, although this bill is apparently supposed to improve the present situation, if we consider the polls in Quebec and elsewhere, it is clear most people are against this kind of reform, because they do not perceive it as such. Now there are polls and polls. The Tories opposite say that the political polls confirm their popularity, but I am talking about the popularity of this particular bill.
March 23, 1993

Government Orders
Let me explain. What strikes me most about this bill is that it is a denial of the basic rights of the consumer, or the policyholder if you prefer. It has often been said that Bill C-113 is basically an insurance contract between employer and employee.
However, I remember that when I was president of the Automobile Protection Association I had to intervene in litigation between insurance companies and policyholders. I can tell you that if this was an insurance contract and I had to advise a consumer, I would tell him never to sign a contract that contains so many denials of basic rights.
I will give you a few examples to show that the so-called improvements in Bill C-113 are likely to make the situation worse and take away basic rights we already have and which are unique.
For instance, in criminal law we can compare this with the rights of a policyholder. It is up to the system to prove the guilt of the accused. This means that the accused is innocent until proven guilty. But as you and I understand Bill C-113, that is not what happens. Under the present unemployment insurance system it is up to the claimant to prove the validity of his claim, and he will receive no money until he has done so.
In criminal law, when there is a doubt the accused is always innocent until proven guilty. In the case of unemployment insurance, the claimant is guilty until he can prove otherwise.
Imagine the case of someone in need of money and acting in good faith when he or she asks the government for help. Now we have a problem, because the government wants to investigate. The investigation may take a week, a month, two months, three months, and during that time, you do not have a cent and your insurance contract-let us call it that-is not paid up. You will get no compensation until the investigators-who are paid for what they do, so they are in no hurry-have finished their work.
This is a pretty serious problem, because the government theoretically-, and I say theoretically, because I can hardly believe the government is all bad and it must have wanted to do the right thing but the difference between theory and practice is staggering.
I remember when people filed claims with their car insurance companies, for example, and that is not as critical as unemployment insurance, but car insurance claims were usually paid in two or three weeks. Most insurance companies pay as soon as they receive the claim. When the government says that payment is made very quickly, in a week or two, I do not agree. We have figures showing that it takes months and months and in that time people are stressed. Most people who have to wait are in a real fix.
I would like to give you another example from the Confederation of National Trade Unions (CSN) in Quebec. The CSN has a striking example: someone works all his life for the same employer, quits his job and then works somewhere else for 15 weeks. That person would be refused benefits if the requirement to work 16 weeks applies. With Bill C-113, the bill before us today, all insurable weeks from the first job would no longer count for anything, even if premiums were collected during those weeks.
Mr. Speaker, if you were a steelworker and had worked for 20 years and decided to change jobs, but had only worked 13 weeks at the new job, you would not be eligible for unemployment insurance. That is not right, even if the Conservatives opposite find it funny. It is not funny. Knowingly putting people in a tight situation is not at all funny. It is shameful.
Instead of criticizing the government all the time, today I would like to give some help to people who want their claims to be processed with some speed and efficiency. I would like to give those who need unemployment insurance some examples or suggestions to have their claims processed better. This comes from a publication by employees of various unemployment insurance centres.
First, they say you must arrive early. If you want good service arrive around 8.45 a.m. and you will probably have better service.
Second, if you want to begin a job retraining course, because you want to change your line of work and do something else, it is best not to apply in January or September because they are really loaded with claims from people in those months. In months other than January and September you have a better chance of obtaining a retraining course. Also, something very

March 23, 1993
Government Orders
important, if you are already receiving UI benefits, you have a better chance of getting one of these courses.
Third, apply very promptly. As soon as you know you will be let go or no longer work for the same company, you should apply right away because your two-week waiting period starts from the time of your application, not the time you lose your job. So apply right away and you will wait at most two weeks.
If you need a cheque because you are really in a bind and do not know what to do you can still ask the government to issue you a cheque right away. They have a 24-hour service and if your claim takes too long and you have bills to pay, ask for a cheque right away.
Finally, and this is very important, if you have problems with unemployment insurance, contact your member of Parliament. Conservative, Liberal or New Democrat, we are able to help you because things do go a little faster and more efficiently when a member of Parliament is involved. Also, you can always appeal. Apparently, about 25 per cent of people win their appeals against the government, so you have one chance in four of winning your claim if you are not satisfied with the decision of the Unemployment Insurance Commission.
Finally, keep a record of everyone you spoke to, because not only politicians forget. UI officials can often forget who you are and what you asked for.
With these suggestions, even if Bill C-113 as now proposed puts you in a bad spot, perhaps in your case you can improve your situation. But one thing is sure. With this Bill C-113 there is no chance of improving your situation.
